summary: Redwood and VectorWave ran a 72-min deep-dive on private deployment hardening. Main focuses: deny-by-default ingress/egress, bastion/jump host patterns, egress proxy vs. firewall, KMS/HSM key custody and rotation, SOC2/ISO touchpoints for audit logs, RBAC/SSO mapping to Redwood roles. Agreed next steps: share runbooks, schedule lab and gather egress allowlist.
topics: Audit logging, SIEM ingestion, and retention (SOC2/ISO)
questions: Can Redwood run in a fully isolated VPC with no public egress?
How are audit logs exported and what retention options do we provide?
What are the recommended HSM/KMS architectures for on-prem private deployments?
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-08-04 15:00 UTC — Duration 1:12. Attendees listed above. Link references: Redwood runbook (shared), local network diagram (customer), SOC2 evidence checklist (Janelle).

[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for carving time, appreciate it. we were told this is mostly SecOps and infra, so Ethan and Maya on the call to get into the weeds.
[00:10] Priya (VectorWave SecOps): yeah thanks, I'm Priya. we run most of our ML inference in a private VPC, and we're looking at Redwood private so we can keep model traffic in our network. main concerns: egress control, key custody, and auditability for SOC2.
[00:24] Ethan (Redwood SE): great, Priya. quick high-level — Redwood Private can be deployed with a customer-managed control plane peered into your VPC, or as an on-prem bundle behind your firewall. We support KMS integrations (cloud KMS, customer HSM) and can route egress through a customer-provided proxy.
[00:40] Leo (CTO): when you say route egress through a proxy — does Redwood ever initiate direct connections outbound? we want deny-by-default egress for the subnet.
[00:49] Maya (Redwood SA): good question — in our typical VPC deployment the inference workers are placed in customer subnets and outbound network calls are disabled by default; you control NAT/egress. we do have optional agents that callback to Redwood control endpoints, but for Private we can use a 0-outbound policy and a controlled egress gateway.
[01:05] Tom (Infra): that 0-outbound approach, does it block things like license checks or model downloads? what about pulling images?
[01:12] Ethan: image pulls — we recommend a dedicated internal registry mirror or an AMI/container image baked into your image repo. model artifacts can be preloaded into local object storage. the default is not to reach out to the public internet. if you need dynamic updates we can do signed artifact pulls through your egress proxy.
[01:30] Priya: ok, so we can ensure nothing leaves our VPC unless explicitly allowed. how do you handle DNS resolution for telemetry and control plane?
[01:37] Maya: we support using private endpoints for control plane mgmt; you can map control-plane FQDNs to private IPs via Route53 private hosted zones or your internal DNS. telemetry can be pushed to your SIEM over TLS to an internal collector.
[01:50] Janelle (Compliance): SOC2 asks for immutable logs and retention policies. how are audit logs stored and can we ship them to our Splunk/ELK?
[01:58] Ethan: yes — Redwood can forward structured audit logs via syslog/HTTPS to your collector. logs include token-level id, route, model version, and request metadata. for Private we also write a local immutable audit ledger that can be snapshot-exported. retention is configurable — default 90 days but we can extend for enterprise.
[02:16] Leo: snapshot-exported — is that tamper-evident? we need chain-of-custody for a few customers.
[02:22] Ethan: the local ledger uses append-only files with checksums; for higher assurance we can integrate with your HSM to sign snapshots. that's part of the HSM integration playbook we have.
[02:31] Priya: can you say more about HSM — we currently use an on-prem Thales HSM. we do not want Redwood to hold our keys.
[02:38] Maya: absolutely. Redwood supports customer-managed keys in two patterns: 1) KMS proxy where we call your KMS over mutual TLS for envelope keys, or 2) HSM-attestation where keys never leave your HSM and signing happens inside your cluster. both can be used for model encryption-at-rest and audit snapshot signing.
[02:55] Tom: about key rotation — we need a rotation schedule and a revocation flow if keys are compromised. do you have documented playbooks?
[03:02] Sofia: Ethan has a doc, but to summarize: we support automatic key rotation for envelope keys with a configurable grace period and can re-encrypt stored artifacts in a rolling fashion. if a primary key is revoked we can fail closed and require re-keying to decrypt cached KV.
[03:18] Speaker 6: sorry, quick interruption, the video feed is fuzzy for me.
[03:22] Priya: no worries. can we dig into ingress — what patterns for the control plane are recommended? we want to minimize public ingress and use mTLS/SSO.
[03:30] Ethan: recommended pattern: control plane endpoints on private IPs, mutual TLS between operator clients and control plane. RBAC hooks into your SAML/SSO provider via SSO or SCIM for identity sync. we also offer a short-lived cert issuing flow for operator tooling.
[03:47] Janelle: for SOC2 we'll need evidence of user access reviews and role mappings — is there an audit export for RBAC changes?
[03:54] Maya: yes, role changes, policy modifications, and SSO provisioning events are logged as discrete audit events and can be exported. we can also produce CSV exports for quarterly access reviews.
[04:05] Priya: great. on network segmentation — we run different security zones: ingest, inference, storage. can Redwood workers be pinned to a particular subnet and not see other zones?
[04:14] Ethan: you can deploy inference workers into specific subnets with strict NetworkPolicy and security group rules. we recommend an additional network interface for management traffic and no cross-zone routing unless explicitly allowed.
[04:27] Tom: curious about egress controls for model telemetry — sometimes our apps call out to external model registries for updates. can we funnel that through an internal egress gateway with per-host allowlists?
[04:35] Maya: yes, the pattern is egress gateway + proxy ACLs. you maintain a small allowlist of canonical destinations. we also support SNI-based filtering and certificate pinning for higher assurance.
[04:48] Leo: what about SNI obfuscation — some proxies do SNI rewriting, does Redwood support passing client certificates through?
[04:55] Ethan: we can do certificate-passthrough when the egress gateway is TLS-terminating inside your boundary; otherwise we support mTLS origination from the worker to the final destination if you want end-to-end identity.
[05:07] Priya: any gotchas with KV cache & secrets? last time we heard KV cache could leak keys in memory under certain configs.
[05:14] Maya: we have mitigations — runtime isolates KV cache per-process, memory locking options, and optional secure enclaves. secrets are never persisted to local disk unencrypted; they sit wrapped with your KMS. but we should run a lab for your specific workload to validate.
[05:30] Sofia: quick commercial note — we also offer Dedicated capacity where Redwood manages the infra but you get isolated GPU pools; that has different tradeoffs for egress and control.
[05:39] Leo: we prefer full control, so Private is likely. what's the upgrade path if we start with Dedicated then move to Private?
[05:46] Ethan: we can migrate tenants and export state; model versions and artifact manifests are portable. the main lift is network and KMS reconfiguration.
[05:55] Tom: firewalling specifics — do you have recommended iptables/iptables rules or do you expect customers to use cloud security groups only?
[06:02] Maya: both. we provide template security group rules for AWS/GCP/Azure and also sample iptables/nftables rules for on-prem. templates include deny-by-default inbound, allow control-plane range, allow egress to registry/proxy, and a high-restriction management port locked to bastion.
[06:20] Priya: bastion — we use ephemeral access via our PAM solution. can we integrate Redwood's operator access into our PAM so ops people don't get raw SSH?
[06:28] Ethan: yes, we can integrate with your bastion/PAM. Redwood's ops tooling issues short-lived certs and we can accept cert-based auth bound to sessions from your PAM. this satisfies least privilege & session recording requirements.
[06:40] Janelle: ISO reviewers asked about vulnerability patch cadence. where do we show patch evidence for the private deploy nodes?
[06:48] Maya: we produce a node-level patching report that includes CVE scanning output and upgrade windows. for Private you own the OS patching — we provide the tooling to automate updates and produce CSV evidence for auditors.
[06:58] Priya: talk to me about the egress deny-by-default scenario with zero public internet. if we want absolutely zero public egress, where do control-plane calls go?
[07:06] Ethan: option A: private peering — control plane endpoints hosted in your VPC or peered VPCs with no NAT. option B: an airgap-style deployment — control plane runs fully on-prem, everything local, no external endpoints. option B requires a slightly different installer but is supported.
[07:24] Leo: for on-prem airgap, how do we handle model updates / security patches? we need an offline artifact signing flow.
[07:30] Maya: we have a signed-artifact bundle flow — Redwood signs bundles which are validated against your local signing keys. or you can fully self-sign. updates happen via USB or secure file transfer, and the runtime validates signatures using either your HSM or our provided verifier.
[07:46] Tom: that signature dance seems important. will you share the verification algorithm & TUF-like metadata?
[07:51] Ethan: yes — we publish a verification spec and can provide a TUF-compatible manifest for you. we'll include that in the runbook.
[07:58] Priya: ok next — data residency. some of our customers require EU-only processing. can we ensure model inference never crosses regions?
[08:06] Maya: you can pin deployments to region-specific capacity and we support geo-fencing of requests. routing policies ensure traffic only stays inside the region and fallback policies can be disabled to avoid cross-region failover.
[08:19] Janelle: also need to prove chain-of-custody for PII — how granular is the audit trail? per-request token-level you said?
[08:26] Ethan: yes, per-request with hashed identifiers if you prefer pseudonymization. timestamps, route, user id (if available), model version, and token counts are recorded. we can redact prompt plaintext for privacy if needed and still keep structural logs for auditing.
[08:42] Priya: nice. want to touch on RBAC mapping — our internal roles are quite granular. do we map SAML groups into Redwood roles or do we want SCIM sync?
[08:50] Maya: both are supported. SCIM sync is handy for granular provisioning and group mappings; SAML can be used for auth and short-lived SSO sessions. we recommend SCIM for automated deprovisioning which auditors like.
[09:02] Leo: any nuance with service accounts? we want machine-to-machine calls for ingestion pipelines with restricted scopes.
[09:09] Ethan: service accounts are first-class — scoped tokens with minimal privileges, short TTLs, and optionally pinned to source IP ranges or signed certs. we can also bind them to workload identity if you're on cloud provider integrations.
[09:22] Priya: about SIEM ingestion — what formats and throughput limits do you support? we run an 8GB/day log ingestion baseline.
[09:30] Maya: we can stream JSON over HTTP(s) in batches, syslog, or push to S3-compatible endpoints for batch shipping. throughput is configurable; for heavy audit traffic we recommend pushing to internal collectors and letting them buffer to Splunk.
[09:44] Tom: for Splunk we want HEC tokens and index routing. supported?
[09:48] Ethan: yep, HEC supported. we include field-level tags to make search easier (model, route, tenant).
[09:55] Priya: ok, let's do a quick run through of a threat scenario: compromised worker VM — what are containment steps?
[10:01] Maya: isolate the subnet, revoke service account tokens (short TTLs help), rotate keys for affected artifacts, and restore from a known-good snapshot. if you use HSM-backed keys we can invalidate envelopes to prevent decryption. our incident runbook walks through forensic evidence capture too.
[10:15] Janelle: forensic capture — can snapshots be time-stamped and signed to satisfy auditors?
[10:20] Ethan: yes, snapshots can be signed by your HSM and include attestation metadata. we also produce a logs bundle for the time window.
[10:28] Priya: any third-party pen-test results? we want proof of running pentests against the runtime.
[10:33] Maya: Redwood publishes summary pentest reports and CVE remediation timelines. for private deployments we can run customer-scoped pentests under an NDA and provide the resulting evidence for SOC2 auditors.
[10:46] Leo: can we get the pentest scope template?
[10:48] Sofia: we'll attach that to the follow-up email.
[10:52] Speaker 6: question — load balancing, do you have per-tenant QOS?
[10:57] Ethan: yes, per-tenant and per-route shaping. on-prem we rely on your LB, but the runtime exposes hints for CPU/GPU affinity and we can throttle by token budget.
[11:09] Priya: let's surface a few low-level configs: 1) what ports need to be open inbound/outbound? 2) are there ephemeral ports for KV cache sync? 3) where do we place health checks?
[11:18] Maya: we'll send a ports matrix — typical control plane ports, optional debug ports locked to management, and KV syncing happens over gRPC on configurable ports. health checks can hit a local admin endpoint and are recommended to be bound to the management interface only.
[11:33] Tom: do you support service mesh in front of workers? we run istio in some clusters.
[11:38] Ethan: we have an istio integration guide; sidecars are supported but we recommend careful mTLS and resource limits to avoid latency spikes.
[11:49] Priya: a weird ask — we sometimes need on-the-fly throttling for legal holds. can Redwood pause request processing at runtime?
[11:56] Maya: yes — we expose a kill-switch and per-route pause. it's audited and reversible only by specified roles.
[12:05] Leo: final compliance question — do you provide a packaged set of artifacts for auditors (SOC2 folder)?
[12:12] Sofia: yes, we prepare an evidence pack that includes architecture diagrams, patching logs, RBAC exports, pentest summaries, and KMS/HSM integration docs.
[12:19] Priya: ok, let's wrap with the immediate next steps and owners.
[12:23] Sofia: action items we captured earlier — Ethan will share a KMS/HSM note, Maya will share ports matrix and iptables samples, Priya to send us their egress allowlist. we'll schedule the lab for HSM integration and an on-prem bastion workshop.
[12:35] Janelle: timeline-wise, we need SOC2 prep evidence by end of September. is that doable?
[12:42] Maya: yes — if we start the lab next week we can produce the evidence artifacts and a remediation backlog in time.
[12:49] Leo: thanks all, appreciate the depth.
[12:52] Sofia: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the runbook link and Docusign for the NDA if needed.
[12:59] Priya: thanks.
[13:02] Meeting end.

Notes on transcript: occasional audio drops at 03:18 and 10:33, speaker 6 is placeholder for a late-joining engineer. Shared artifacts: https://redwood.internal/runbooks/private-vpc-kms (Redwood runbook), VectorWave-network-diagram-v2 (customer doc).
